newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST-Riksbank to cut repo to 3.80 pct in 3 mth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Riksbank to cut repo to 3.80 pct in 3 mth.

text.p: The Riksbank was expected to lower its key interest rate, the repo rate, on Tuesday and continue easing rates for the next three months, a Reuters poll of 16 analysts showed on Monday.

The chances of this were boosted by last Thursday's consumer price index figures which showed a fall of 0.3 percent in November. For the second consecutive month this gave a negative inflation trend for the past 12 months.

One analyst said the market took this as further confirmation that the central bank would lower its repo rate on December 17 from the current rate of 4.35 percent when it sets a new operation for three weeks to cover the holiday period.
"There is deflation now and this is the reason that we believe the Riksbank will continue to lower the repo rate. The Riksbank is in line with the inflation target for next year," said one analyst.
With most analysts expecting a cut of 20-25 basis points on Tuesday, they forecast that over the next three months the Riksbank would lower the repo rate to about 3.80 percent.
The repo, the Riksbank's key tool for controlling money market liquidity and the central rate in a three-tier system, began 1996 at 8.91 percent but has been cut regularly since.
Analysts on average expected the repo rate to hit bottom in the first quarter of 1997 with forecasts ranging between 3.50-4.00 percent.
In a year's time however the repo rate is expected to have risen slightly but only one of the economists questioned thought it would be higher than today's level.
The average estimate was for the repo rate to be at around 4.0 percent in a year's time with forecasts varying betwen 3.75-4.50 percent.
Swedish debt yields are expected to fall in the short term but are also expected in a year's time to be above today's levels, the poll showed.
"We are expecting strong growth in 1997 and 1998. Monetary policy will be directed by inflation and so I think it will be difficult to maintain low yields," said Jan Haggstrom from Handelsbanken.
Six-month T-bill rates are expected to fall by around 10 basis points to 3.75 percent over the next three months from the current 3.86 percent but forecasts ranged between 3.40-4.05 percent.
In a year's time the rates on six-month T-bills were seen at 3.50-4.60 percent.

At the long end of the yield curve bond yields are expected to fall about 10 basis points in the short term but will eventually be driven up against by higher international yields and strong world economic growth.
In three months, the ten year bond yield was seen at between 6.50-7.50 percent and in a year at 6.10-7.90 percent.

"You can speculate about whether or not the Bundesbank will lift its rates by the end of next year. If it does the Riksbank will follow. You can also say that general economic change will be the impetus behind higher yields," said an economist.
Worries about inflation and yield rises in the U.S. are other reasons that make economists expect rates to go up over time.
The crown is expected to be stable against the mark in the short and long term.
"The only black cloud is the Swedish attitude to the EMU question but I don't see any big risk factors," said Ian Ganna, economist at Chase Investment Bank.
